li.a: SlashGear: A Brief History Of The Warlocks Motorcycle Club
One Percenter Bikers: Warlocks MC (Motorcycle Club - Florida)
Bobber Brothers: Warlocks MC, The Florida and Pennsylvania Clubs
US Court of Appeals, 11th Circuit, via Justia (Internet Archive copy): United States v. Bowman, 302 F.3d 1228 (2002)
US District Court, Middle District of Florida: The Outlaws, Bikers Behind Bars
Global News: Members of Warlocks outlaw motorcycle gang arrested in Drayton Valley

content.p: The Warlocks Motorcycle Club of Florida is a one-percenter club (SlashGear traces the term to a 1947 remark that 99 percent of motorcycle clubs were law-abiding) that traces itself to 1967 and to a mother chapter in the Lockhart district of Orlando. Its public record is thin. Most of what is written about it online is recycled club lore, and the clearest window into its violent years comes not from the club or its members but from a federal appeals court. That court was describing a case against someone else: the leader of the rival Outlaws club, who was convicted of ordering a murder of a Warlocks chapter president and the bombing of a Warlocks clubhouse.
A second, unrelated club called the Warlocks exists in and around Philadelphia. Reports about the two are mixed up constantly, and the sections below deal only with the Florida club.

The founding account that circulates is a naval one. According to One Percenter Bikers, thirteen men aboard the carrier USS Shangri-La, on an eight-month tour in February 1967, discussed starting a motorcycle club once they were home. They settled on the name Warlocks and a phoenix design, and each was to open a chapter in his own town. Only one of them followed through, according to that account: Tommy "Grub" Freeland, who started the Orlando chapter at Lockhart. SlashGear tells it almost identically but names the founder as Thomas Freeman Jr., and places the story at the end of the 1960s as the ship's deployment with the Sixth Fleet was ending. SlashGear adds that, according to reports, he stayed active in club affairs until he died in 2019.

The story is weaker than it sounds. Bobber Brothers points out that it traces back to the club and people close to it rather than to any Navy record, and that accounts disagree on how many sailors were involved and on when the talk began. It adds that even the founding city is open to question: Lockhart and Orlando are the usual answers, but one reference work gives Jacksonville Beach. It prefers to call the tale club history rather than verified chronology.

The name itself is disputed. Members of the Pennsylvania club hold that the Florida men picked up "Warlocks" while visiting the Philadelphia Navy Yards in the late 1960s, and so consider the name stolen. The Florida club says it chose the name aboard ship. Bobber Brothers notes that no document settles the question and that both versions come from the clubs themselves.

The club's emblem is a phoenix, also called the "warbird", usually described as an eagle between curved text bars. The Philadelphia club wears a harpy instead, which is why it is sometimes called the Harpy Warlocks. Colors are listed as red, orange and gold by SlashGear and as orange, red, gold and black by Bobber Brothers. The initials WFFW stand for "Warlocks Forever, Forever Warlocks". Another slogan, reported by both SlashGear and One Percenter Bikers, runs: "To find us, you must be good. To catch us, you must be fast. To beat us, you must be kidding."

SlashGear says the club has more than 500 members, a figure it labels as an estimate that varies, and gives Florida eleven chapters, South Carolina seven and Virginia five, with chapters abroad in Germany, Canada and the United Kingdom. Bobber Brothers declines to use such totals, arguing that enthusiast sites publish exact numbers that cannot be traced to a court filing, agency report or contemporary news story. The honest position is that nobody outside the club has published a verified count.

The most serious violence in the club's documented history began in a garage on 21 February 1991. Raymond "Bear" Chaffin, leader of a Warlocks chapter, was shot four times and killed. Where he lived is given two ways: the court that later described the crime placed him in Edgewater, while One Percenter Bikers says New Smyrna Beach. One Percenter Bikers says he was working on his Harley-Davidson when he was shot, and that his daughter found him when she came home from school.

The Eleventh Circuit's account, drawn from the trial of Outlaws international president Harry "Taco" Bowman, is more detailed. Prosecutors' evidence, as the court summarised it, was that in the early 1990s the Warlocks allied with the Hell's Angels and began selling drugs for them, which started a war with the Outlaws. Chaffin had once been an Outlaw himself. According to that evidence, Bowman told Wayne "Joe Black" Hicks, the Outlaws' Florida regional president, to find Chaffin and kill him. An Outlaws probationary member, Alex "Dirt" Ankerich, was sent to spend a night at Chaffin's home without revealing his club, the court recorded, and was then directed with Fort Lauderdale president Houston Murphy to carry out the killing. The court said Ankerich shot Chaffin four times in the back of the head with a .22 pistol fitted with a silencer, and that newspaper reports of the murder were mailed to other Outlaws chapters. Hicks became a government informant, according to One Percenter Bikers.

Bowman was later convicted of racketeering, and the murder of Chaffin was among the racketeering acts the court listed against him. The opinion records what was proved against Bowman; it is not a verdict on every other person it names.

The Warlocks were also the target of a federal infiltration. One Percenter Bikers says that 41 Warlocks members and associates were arrested in March 1991 after a long operation by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and that 18 of the arrests concerned the sale to agents of two dozen machine guns and more than 80 homemade bombs. The rest were on weapons, drugs and stolen-property charges. SlashGear says the arrests were made around Chaffin's funeral. Neither gives a court record.

According to the same site, an agent named Steve Martin befriended the club's president, John "Spike" Ingrao, at a gym in Apopka. He became a patched member without first serving as a probationary member, on the promise that he would found a Fort Lauderdale chapter, and used it to bring in four other law-enforcement officers. The operation ended, the site says, over agent safety concerns after Chaffin's death. Ingrao was sentenced to nine years in prison, according to One Percenter Bikers; SlashGear spells his name Ingrano and says almost a decade. SlashGear adds that a Florida chapter, whose president was Chaffin, had been in negotiations with the Hell's Angels and discussing a "patch over" with another club, the Boozefighters, before his death.

The appeals opinion records a second chapter of the Outlaws' war. In 1994, it says, Bowman told Outlaws to do whatever they could to destroy the Warlocks. Hicks asked Stephen "DK" Lemunyon, a Daytona Outlaw, to work out how to destroy the Warlocks clubhouse in Orlando. Lemunyon and another man built a bomb, the court said, and it was detonated in October 1994 by Lemunyon, Steve Hilton and Louis Musher. Bowman, it recorded, told Florida Outlaws he was proud of the work and urged them to keep watching and killing Warlocks.

A few months later, the court said, four Daytona Outlaws planned a second firebombing, aimed at the Warlocks clubhouse in Brevard County. That plan failed when authorities arrested the men and seized the device during a search of Lemunyon's home.

Bowman was indicted in 1997, became a fugitive on the FBI's ten-most-wanted list and was arrested on 7 June 1999 in Sterling Heights, Michigan. His 2001 trial in Tampa ended in convictions for racketeering, conspiracy to commit murder, and drug and firearm offences, and a sentence of life in prison. The racketeering acts the appeals court listed included the bombing of the Orlando Warlocks clubhouse, the conspiracy to bomb the Brevard one, and a conspiracy to murder members of the Warlocks. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed in 2002.

Bobber Brothers, summarising contemporary reporting, describes the best-documented federal action against the Florida club as a July 2003 ATF operation, the end of a two-year undercover investigation. It reached across Florida, Virginia, West Virginia, New York, Maryland and South Carolina and produced 34 arrests and nearly 50 searches. Authorities reported recovering more than 120 firearms, over $25,000, body armor and quantities of methamphetamine, cocaine and marijuana. Bobber Brothers stresses these are investigation-wide totals, not convictions. It also notes that federal searches were carried out against Hells Angels members in Maryland as part of the wider case, and that the 2003 coverage mentioned a national president for the Warlocks.

In March 2014, the Alberta Law Enforcement Response Teams arrested four members and four associates of the club's Drayton Valley chapter after a search of a home on 21 March. Global News named the members as King (31), Buzzell (49), Bushell (22) and McKnight (41), with the first names Sheldon, Rocky, Luke and Dean. Between them and the four associates, eight people faced 77 drug and weapons charges in all. An ALERT inspector, Darcy Strang, said the Warlocks were a larger group operating in the United States that first appeared in Alberta in November 2010. The reports reviewed here do not give the outcome of those cases.

More recent Florida episodes are thinly sourced. Bobber Brothers cites Titusville police reports of arrests in 2024 after a confrontation involving a person police identified as a Warlocks member and three they identified as Mongols members. SlashGear describes a July 2025 clash before a planned group ride in Daytona Beach in which, it says, the Mongols surrounded the Warlocks, shots were fired and a nearby hospital locked down. It cites no police or court record, and the reports reviewed here do not give charges or outcomes.

Bobber Brothers adds two cautions that apply to the whole record. Charges are allegations until a court rules, and a conviction is a finding about one person, not about everyone who wears a patch. The club's own position, it says, as with most such clubs, is that it is a motorcycle club and not a criminal organization.
